planting.note: Direct sow in spring into gypseous clay, caliche, or gravelly, low-fertility soil in full sun; this low subshrub needs sharp drainage and no supplemental fertility to thrive on raw mineral ground.

directions: Fanmustard forms a woody-based clump of narrow gray-green leaves topped by loose spikes of four-petaled white flowers that age to lavender as they fade. It is one of the more widespread gypsum-tolerant wildflowers of the Chihuahuan Desert, equally at home on bare clay flats, gravelly knolls, and gypsum outcrops, and it blooms intermittently almost year-round where winters stay mild. In the garden it works as a long-season filler in a mineral scree or gravel bed, needing nothing beyond excellent drainage and full sun. Shear spent flower stalks back by half after a bloom flush to keep the clump tidy and encourage rebloom.

subcategory: gypsum and sandy-soil Chihuahuan Desert wildflower

planting.note: Broadcast seed in fall onto lean, gypseous or sandy, well-drained soil in full sun so winter moisture and cold stratify it naturally; established clumps spread by shallow rhizomes.

directions: Crownleaf evening primrose has deeply comb-cut, fern-like leaves and low mounds of white, four-petaled flowers that open in late afternoon and fade to pink by the next morning. It ranges from the northern Great Plains south onto Chihuahuan Desert gypsum and sandy flats, and its spreading rhizomes let it knit together loose, eroding ground. Plant it in a dry rock garden or gravel border where its white, moth-pollinated flowers can be appreciated at dusk, and leave the papery seed capsules in place over winter for self-sowing. It needs no irrigation once established and resents rich, moisture-retentive soil.

planting.note: Scatter seed in fall over bare, raw gypsum or caliche gravel in full sun; this low dryland stickleaf needs mineral soil with almost no organic matter and overwinter chilling to germinate well.

directions: Gypsum blazingstar is a dwarf, gray-leaved relative of the showier blazingstars, forming compact tufts on raw gypsum and caliche outcrops across the southwestern US. Its five-petaled, pale yellow flowers open in bright sun and are followed by barrel-shaped capsules; the rough, barbed-haired leaves cling readily to clothing and gloves. It is best used as a specimen or small colony in a mineral scree bed or trough garden rather than a mixed border, since it quickly declines in fertile or regularly watered soil. Leave seed capsules intact through winter to allow self-sowing into bare gaps.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring into gypseous sand or sand-dune soil in full sun; this rare regional blanketflower needs the same sharp drainage as common Gaillardia but tolerates far leaner, more mineral ground.

directions: Gypsum blanketflower is a narrow regional endemic of gypsum outcrops and gypsum sand dunes in Arizona, New Mexico, and West Texas, forming a low subshrub with leafy stems rather than the basal-leaved rosette typical of common blanketflower. Flower heads carry a ring of red-orange rays around a dense button of yellow disc flowers tipped in purple, held well above the foliage on wiry stalks. Because wild populations are scattered and locally uncommon, source seed only from reputable native-plant or regional wildflower suppliers rather than wild collecting. In the garden it performs best in a gritty, mineral bed that mimics its gypsum habitat and resents winter wet.

planting.note: Broadcast seed in spring onto raw gypsum sand or alkaline gravelly soil in full sun; it forms a non-rhizomatous tuft and does not spread aggressively, making it suitable for restoration seeding or a dryland garden accent.

directions: Gyp dropseed is a wiry, tuft-forming bunchgrass of gypsum and alkaline sandy soils across the desert Southwest, with stiff basal blades that splay out nearly perpendicular to the stem and small open seedheads in late summer. Because it stays in a tight clump without rhizomes, it is useful for stabilizing bare, mineral-rich ground without becoming invasive in a planted bed. Use it as a fine-textured accent among boulders or in a gravel garden, or include it in native seed mixes for erosion control on disturbed gypsum or caliche sites. It needs essentially no irrigation once established and declines in rich garden soil.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring into gypsum or strongly gypseous soil in full sun; this woody-taprooted mat former is intolerant of regular watering or competition and needs completely open, mineral ground to establish.

directions: Gypsum crinklemat forms a dense, bristly gray-green mat of tiny linear leaves hugging gypsum and heavily gypseous ground in New Mexico and West Texas, flowering with small, inconspicuous pink tubular blooms tucked into the leaf axils from late spring to summer. Its tight, woody-based mat makes it a useful living mulch between flagstones or boulders in a mineral scree garden, where it covers bare gypsum chips better than turf could. It is slow to establish and best planted from small plugs or seed into undisturbed mineral soil rather than amended garden beds. Avoid overhead irrigation, which quickly rots the crown in humid conditions.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring into dry, deep gypsum sand in full sun; this subshrub is considered a reliable indicator of gypsum soils and fails outside mineral, fast-draining ground.

directions: Gypsum nama is a woody-based little subshrub with fleshy, rolled-edge leaves crowded along the stems and small clusters of whitish, funnel-shaped flowers blooming through the hot months. It occurs almost exclusively on gypsum sand in central and eastern New Mexico and West Texas, making it a dependable marker of true gypsophile habitat. Grow it in a dedicated gypsum-chip or mineral scree bed alongside other gypsum specialists, since it struggles and fades in ordinary garden loam. It is best left dry between rains and needs no feeding or mulching once established.
